job.style: a passage rich in numbers, dates or measurements

passage: The Delhi Sultanate was not the first time Muslim rulers entered India, as trade and cultural exchanges had occurred for centuries before the 13th century. Once established, the Sultans relied on 'Bandagan', or military slaves, who were trained to hold high political offices rather than perform manual household chores. These officials were often assigned an 'Iqta', a tract of land that they managed for the Sultan. A Muqti was the holder of this land, but their position was strictly non-hereditary; they were frequently transferred to prevent them from claiming permanent ownership. To maintain control over the vast empire, the Sultans built garrison towns, which were fortified settlements designed specifically for soldiers, not for general trade or civilian living. Alauddin Khalji implemented strict market reforms, not out of charity for the poor, but to keep the prices of essential goods low so he could maintain a large, standing army at a lower cost. Later, Muhammad bin Tughluq introduced token currency made of cheap metals. This policy failed not because people were uneducated, but because the government could not prevent citizens from minting their own counterfeit coins at home, which devalued the currency. These administrative decisions were calculated attempts to centralize power, rather than the erratic actions of a ruler who had lost his mind.

items.evidence: Once established, the Sultans relied on 'Bandagan', or military slaves, who were trained to hold high political offices rather than perform manual household chores.
items.q: A Sultan's slave is made a governor. Why is this not surprising?
options: Bandagan were trained for high offices
Bandagan were trained as household servants
Bandagan were freed once they served
Bandagan were the Sultan's own sons
items.explain: Bandagan were military slaves trained to hold high political offices, not to do household chores.

wrong.why: thinks slaves only did household chores
thinks a slave must be freed before ruling
thinks high office needs royal birth

items.evidence: A Muqti was the holder of this land, but their position was strictly non-hereditary; they were frequently transferred to prevent them from claiming permanent ownership.
items.q: Why did the Sultan often move a Muqti to a new Iqta?
options: To keep him from claiming the land
To let his son take over the land
To make him pay the Iqta as tax
To let him rule the land as owner
items.explain: Muqtis were transferred often so they could not claim permanent ownership of the land.

wrong.why: thinks the Muqti's post passed to his son
thinks Iqta was a religious tax
thinks Muqtis owned their Iqta land

items.evidence: To maintain control over the vast empire, the Sultans built garrison towns, which were fortified settlements designed specifically for soldiers, not for general trade or civilian living.
items.q: A trader wants to set up a shop freely. Would a garrison town suit him?
options: No, it was built mainly for soldiers
No, it was built only for Muqtis
Yes, it was an open city for trade
Yes, it was built to house peasants
items.explain: Garrison towns were fortified settlements for soldiers, not meant for general trade or civilian living.

wrong.why: thinks garrison towns were open trading cities
thinks civilians lived in the garrison towns

items.evidence: Alauddin Khalji implemented strict market reforms, not out of charity for the poor, but to keep the prices of essential goods low so he could maintain a large, standing army at a lower cost.
items.q: Why did Alauddin Khalji keep the prices of essential goods low?
options: To support a large army cheaply
To help poor people of Delhi
To make traders richer in Delhi
To punish Muqtis who kept land
items.explain: Low prices let Alauddin maintain a large standing army at lower cost, not help the poor.

wrong.why: thinks the reforms were charity for the poor
thinks lower prices were meant to benefit traders
mixes the reforms up with the Muqti land system

items.evidence: This policy failed not because people were uneducated, but because the government could not prevent citizens from minting their own counterfeit coins at home, which devalued the currency.
items.q: Why did Muhammad bin Tughluq's token coins lose their value?
options: Citizens made fake coins at home
People did not understand money yet
The cheap metal was too heavy to carry
The capital was moved to Daulatabad
items.explain: The government could not stop people minting counterfeit coins at home, which devalued the currency.

wrong.why: thinks people did not understand money
picks a detail about cheap metal that is not the cause
mixes in the capital shift as a cause
